pl-l3d30c1-d1e115.summary: Asks which is better and more meritorious, to love friends or to love enemies.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e118.summary: Notes that the comparison is complex. If love of friends alone is compared with love of friends and enemies, the answer is clear. But if one asks within one person who loves both which is better, the answer is obscure, since it concerns a movement of the mind: whether one movement is more intense toward the friend, or two, one toward the enemy, called more difficult, and one toward the friend, which seems more fervent. The more fervent may not unfittingly be thought better.
claims: Loving friends and enemies is better than loving friends alone.
Within one person the comparison is obscure.
The more fervent love may be judged better.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e121.summary: Notes that Augustine seems to hold that loving an enemy is greater than loving a friend, since he says it belongs to the perfect. Quoting the Enchiridion at length: it is great to be kind to one who has done no harm, but far greater to love one's enemy; this belongs to the perfect sons of God, toward which every believer should strive. Since not all who are heard in 'forgive us our debts' have such perfection, the promise is fulfilled if one who does not yet love his enemy forgives from the heart one who asks; one who asks forgiveness is no longer to be counted an enemy, and whoever does not forgive the penitent should not expect God's forgiveness.
claims: Loving enemies belongs to the perfect.
The promise of the Lord's Prayer is fulfilled by forgiving those who ask.
Whoever does not forgive the penitent will not be forgiven.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e149.summary: Draws out that this seems to show that loving and doing good to an enemy is of greater virtue than loving one who has done no harm, or a friend.
claims: Loving an enemy seems of greater virtue than loving a friend.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e152.summary: Adds that if someone refuses this simply, saying a friend is loved more intensely, he should interpret it as above: the comparison is between love of the friend alone and love of both friend and enemy.
claims: The comparison is between loving friends only and loving both.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e155.summary: Raises a greater difficulty in Augustine's claim that loving enemies does not belong to all those heard in the Lord's Prayer: it implies that God forgives sins to one who does not love his enemy, if he forgives a brother who asks. Since sins are not forgiven an adult without charity, such a person has charity without loving enemies. Yet if every man is neighbor, the enemy is too, and the general commandment orders all to love all, including enemies.
claims: Sins are not forgiven an adult without charity.
Since the enemy is a neighbor, all are commanded to love enemies.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e166.summary: Reports that some, taking Augustine's words simply, qualify the commandment: loving every man, including enemies, is a precept for the perfect; for lesser people it is a counsel, while the precept is to love those who have done no harm and not to hate enemies.
claims: Some hold that loving enemies is a precept for the perfect and a counsel for others.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e169.summary: Prefers that the commandment orders all to love everyone, including enemies, as the authorities above and many others attest.
claims: All are commanded to love enemies.

pl-l3d30c1-d1e172.summary: Interprets Augustine's last words as concerning perfect charity, belonging only to the perfect, who love friends and enemies perfectly and do them good; this perfection is not shared by all heard in the Lord's Prayer. Likewise, fulfilling the promise without yet loving the enemy refers to perfect love.
claims: Augustine refers to perfect love of enemies, not to love as such.

pl-l3d30c1.summary: Asks whether it is better and more meritorious to love friends or enemies. Comparing love of friends alone with love of friends and enemies, the answer is clear; within one person loving both, it is obscure whether one movement or two is at stake, and the more fervent may be better. Augustine seems to hold that loving enemies is greater, belonging to the perfect, and that many fulfil the Lord's Prayer by forgiving those who ask without yet loving enemies. This troubles Lombard: since sins are not forgiven an adult without charity, one would have charity without loving enemies, though the commandment of neighbor-love includes enemies. Some answer that loving enemies is a precept for the perfect and a counsel for the lesser. Lombard prefers that all are commanded to love enemies, and reads Augustine as speaking of perfect love of enemies.
claims: Loving friends and enemies is better than loving friends only.
Within one person the comparison is obscure because it concerns movements of the mind.
Loving enemies perfectly belongs to the perfect.
All are commanded to love their enemies.
Augustine's statement concerns the perfect love of enemies, not love as such.
